newsitem.title: UK: London palladium prices climb on Russian fears.
newsitem.headline: London palladium prices climb on Russian fears.

text.p: Palladium prices firmed to their highest in nearly four months on Thursday on Russian supply concerns and prospects of rising consumer demand, and despite a drop in values for gold and other precious metals.
Dealers cited a combination of questions over Russia's ability to fulfil its first months' deliveries against annual supply contracts and the rising consumer demand.
Palladium was fixed at $122.25 per ounce, up $2.25 overnight and matching its highest fixing since September 16, 1996.
"There is a concern about Russia not being able to deliver and some consumers don't expect to receive metal," one platinum group metals analyst said.

The feeling in the industry was that Russia had not sorted out its personnel problems in Moscow after disbanding the precious metals and stones export agency which handled palladium exports last year, analysts and dealers said.
Annual supply contracts have not been signed yet, leading to consumers seeking cover against first quarter deliveries.
"It looks like there will be a gap in delivery. I have heard the Russia might be going to miss out a month or might make up for it in the second month. It's not clear," the analyst said.
Meanwhile consumers and speculators were buying in an already tight market against the possibility of a shortfall.
Russia's principal contracts are with the Japanese electronics companies and autocatalyst makers.
Demand from the electronic industry was down last year reflecting a build up of stocks of finished goods, but early signs are that palladium demand will revive in 1997.
"The electronics market appears to be picking up again this year although it may not recover to 1995 levels," an industry analyst said.

Johnson Matthey (JM), the leading refiner of platinum group metals, estimated electronics applications used 2.12 million ounces of palladium last year against 2.65 million in 1995 - out of world demand of 6.1 million ounces.
Palladium's consumption in autocatalysts was estimated at 2.27 million ounces last year, up 31 per cent versus 1995.

The boost in palladium use by the car makers reflected its better cost effectiveness against more expensive platinum and increasingly tight legislation on car emission standards in Europe and North America, market analysts said.
"We have seen good buying from the U.S. car makers especially in the past few days," said a London-based platinum group metals trader.

He noted that sponge grade material - the grade favoured for autocatalysts - was commanding a $2.50 per ounce premium over plate in North America and $1.00 in Europe, reflecting the cost of shipping it across the Atlantic.
"The Russians don't want to see palladium rocket up as they are aware that the electronics companies could substitute nickel," an analyst said.
Palladium reached its recent highs in April 1995 when it fixed on April 5 at $178.25, its highest fixing since April 1989, before increased sales from Russia brought prices lower.
Johnson Matthey estimated Russia exports last year at 3.8 mllion ounces out of world supply of 5.98 million ounces.
It also calculated that about 50 percent of the Russian export was made up of supplies from its national stockpile.
